items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' and never set an agenda. The closest thing to a roadmap came from the customer, not the rep — she offered 'so let me, let you ask questions unless you want me to just explain the situation' and Lukas took the passive option: 'oh, you could just explain the situation I could kind of throw my questions in when they come up.' That worked out because she is an organized caller, but he surrendered the structure of the call to her and never confirmed a plan or a timeframe.
Special considerations never asked — no narrow stairwell, no tight turn at the top of the stairs, no long carry, on a load that includes a bed and nightstand coming down from the second floor.

Access concerns never asked at the storage facility: no gate code, no truck access, no drive-up versus interior unit, no hours restriction. He confirmed the unit is on the first floor and that it is a 10x15, and stopped there. Storage facility access is a classic hidden time sink and it was left open.
Additional stops never asked. She mentioned she is not moving out the same day, which is exactly the circumstance that sometimes produces a second trip.
Moving stressors never asked.

No hourly rate was ever stated. He quoted totals only — '$480 for a two man crew' at the minimum and '$576' at three hours — which resolve to $192 an hour for the team, or $96 per mover, neither of which he said. She cannot model anything herself from those two data points, and it also made his own fifteen-minute-proration example harder to follow than it needed to be ('$245 or $315 or something like that').
No 'pricing is super simple' opener.

What's included was never proactively stated — the customer had to verify it herself off the emailed estimate: 'to verify what I read on your estimate was that offer does include taxes and everything. So no surprise charges other than the minutes and stuff and then, and they do have the supplies like you said for wrapping or whatever.' He confirmed with 'Correct' and moved on. Gas, truck, taxes, insurance, pads, bands and tools were never listed by the rep on this call.

Disassembly and reassembly were never stated as included at no charge, even though she asked directly about the recliner clips and he confirmed the crew can handle it. She still does not know whether that costs extra.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned — no $2,000, no repair/replace/reimburse, no 60¢/lb baseline. She is putting her furniture into a storage unit, which is the scenario where damage coverage questions surface most often.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned, on a call that booked.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — and this is the single most costly differentiator miss in the entire batch. She works night shift and told him she is going to stay awake after work rather than sleep, specifically so she can be there: 'I need morning cause I work night and so it's, I just I'm just gonna stay up and wait for them to get here.' He booked her an 8:30 AM start. A customer who is burning a night's sleep on the arrival window is the perfect audience for 'and if we miss that window, we start discounting immediately.' It never came.

No 'no hidden fees' pitch, and he introduced a fee without one. The $12-per-pad deposit was volunteered honestly and explained well, but it landed in a conversation where the customer had just asked whether there were surprise charges — the right frame was 'no credit card fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees; the one optional thing is a refundable pad deposit.'
Clock start was never explained — she was never told the clock begins when the crew arrives and the contract opens, or when it stops. The minimum and the proration were both covered clearly.
No sense-check anywhere. 'I just don't like to make promises, I can't keep' is honest but it is not 'does that make sense?', and the estimate block ran without a single check-in.

Stairs never factored into the estimate. She told him 'my bed and the night stand are upstairs' and the two-story carry never appeared in his hours reasoning, which matters because he then quoted the absolute minimum.
Walk distance never asked at either end, and no equivalents used to make the hours concrete.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10, and she was already doing it. She told him unprompted 'my personal family pictures and things, and I'm gonna move those myself in my car' and 'if I have everything ready, I really think we could probably get it done within that two hours.' She raised prep and carloading herself, and the rep never affirmed either as the money-saver it is, never gave her the consolidation list, and never closed with 'does that make sense?'. The nearest thing on the call is the pad-deposit pitch, which is the same economic logic — 'spend a little bit of money to save money on two different ends' — applied to a different lever.

No bolded-details framing on the confirmation email, and the reply ask was for questions rather than corrections: 'you can respond to the email that we sent over to you in the next few minutes and we can answer those questions from there.' On a booking where the whole point of the call was that the previous estimate was wrong, 'reply if anything in there is still off' was the natural close.
Business hours never given.
Customer's name never used once. She introduced herself in her first sentence — 'this is Jennie Walker' — and he never said it again across eight minutes.
top_strength: Lukas did the hardest and most valuable thing on this board: a customer called to say his company's estimate was too high, and he agreed with her and lowered it. She opened with 'when I was looking at the quote or the estimate it was definitely overbooked,' and instead of defending the number or hedging, he listened to a long unstructured description of her belongings and then rebuilt the estimate out loud with his reasoning exposed: 'Main variable I would say is in play would be like the box count give or take... Those we typically see like you know, fifteen to 25 boxes... it does sound like we're probably gonna be like middle to lower end of that spectrum.' Then he named the drivers in the right direction — 'unloads into storage are typically pretty quick and honestly and like load ups the main time... the main thing that's gonna take time would just be wrapping the items' — and landed on the minimum: 'I think it would fall anywhere between that two and a half hour minimum and if it does go a little bit over maybe three hours but that's kind of pushing it realistically speaking.' He gave both dollar figures, explained proration so she understood the downside was protected, and then capped it with a line that is worth teaching verbatim: 'the estimate is not set in stone but as I mentioned I think the minimum is pretty doable in this situation. I just don't like to make promises, I can't keep.' That is credibility built by giving away revenue, and the customer's response — 'Oh, no, I know. It's not my first move and using moving companies' — is the sound of a skeptical caller deciding to trust him. His second strength is proactive transparency where most reps stay quiet. Nobody asked about pad deposits; he raised it himself, framed it honestly as a cost ('I'll just be up forward with you'), explained the refund mechanism both ways — returned pads discount the next move, or bring them to the office for a check — and then made the case on the customer's economics rather than Einstein's: 'it does make the load into storage faster. And it would make the move out of storage faster as well. So, ultimately, spend a little bit of money to save money on two different ends.' His close was clean and complete: availability offered both ways, no-deposit and no-change-fee stated together as a single reassurance ('we don't require any deposit to get you on the schedule and then the event we do need to like change the date around there's no any additional fees to get your date changed as well'), addresses and unit details confirmed back, a specific start time booked, and an email promised within minutes. And he listened well enough to finish her thought about the night shift before she did — 'You have to, you know, fall sleep and wake back up again. Oh, oh, I actually understand that.'
coaching_note: Estimate accuracy: log this one as the strongest positive in the batch and pull the actual against it on September 21st. Amanda's #3 priority is a padding problem, and this is a rep doing the opposite under the exact conditions where padding is tempting — an inbound complaint that the estimate is too high, an unstructured inventory description, and no way to verify. He re-scoped, quoted the minimum, said why, and did not hedge upward to protect himself. If it lands at two and a half to three hours, this call is a training example. Now the gap, and it is a big one: Pricing scored 4/20 on a call that booked. He sold the job on reasonableness alone and never sold Einstein. In eight minutes the customer heard no hourly rate, no what's-included list from the rep's own mouth, no No Worries Damage Coverage, no Meet Your Mover, no On-Time Guarantee, and no no-hidden-fees pitch — she had to read the included-taxes item off the old email and ask him to confirm it. The pattern is that Lukas is excellent at responding and weak at initiating: every piece of pricing content on this call was either triggered by her question or omitted. Fix: the differentiator block is not optional and it is not contingent on the customer asking. Even on a warm callback that is going to book, run it — 'and everything's in the rate: truck, gas, taxes, all the wrap and pads, all the disassembly and reassembly. Every move carries No Worries Damage Coverage, up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse, where most movers give you sixty cents a pound. A few days out you'll get an email introducing your actual crew with their photo. And if we ever miss your arrival window we start discounting immediately.' That is forty seconds and it takes this section from 4/20 to something like 14/20 without changing anything else about the call. Highest-value single line he missed: the On-Time Guarantee. She told him she works nights and is going to skip sleeping in order to be there at 8:30. Nobody in this batch had a better reason to hear that guarantee, and it is the kind of detail that turns a satisfied customer into a referring one. Second: the Save Your Ass speech is a zero on a customer who volunteered both halves of it herself — she is carloading her own family photos and she told him she thinks it can be done inside two hours if she has everything ready. All he had to do was affirm and extend: 'Exactly right, and lean into that — anything small and loose you can take over in the car yourself comes straight off the clock, and having the boxes stacked near the garage door before we get there is worth fifteen or twenty minutes on its own. Does that make sense?' That also protects his own aggressive estimate, which is the neat part: the prep speech and the tight quote reinforce each other. Third, small but repeated across the board: use her name. She gave it in her first sentence and he never said it once.
phone_presence_notes: Relaxed and genuinely listening rather than processing — he normalized her recliner worry without condescension ('It's something we see fairly frequently. So it shouldn't be like out of the ordinary'), completed her night-shift reasoning before she finished it ('You have to, you know, fall sleep and wake back up again. Oh, oh, I actually understand that'), and built credibility with 'I just don't like to make promises, I can't keep'; short of a 5 only because her name was never used and there was no warm-up or humor beat.
